name: Serotonin
role: Carries messages between nerve cells in the brain and gut. It is involved in mood, sleep, appetite and digestion. Mood is shaped by many things at once, so serotonin is one part of the picture, not the whole story.
supportedBy: Daylight, regular movement, enough sleep and regular meals are linked to healthy serotonin activity.

name: Dopamine
role: Part of the brain's reward and motivation system. It is also involved in movement, attention and learning.
supportedBy: Exercise, enough sleep and finishing small goals are linked to healthy dopamine signalling.

name: Noradrenaline
role: Drives the fight-or-flight response: it raises heart rate, alertness and attention when you are stressed or in danger. Also called norepinephrine.
supportedBy: Slow breathing, movement and sleep help the stress response settle after it has been switched on.

name: Cortisol
role: The main stress hormone. It helps you wake up, manages how the body uses energy and responds to stress. It is normally high in the morning and low at night.
supportedBy: Short sleep, long-lasting stress and a lot of caffeine are linked to higher cortisol. A regular sleep schedule supports its daily rhythm.

name: GABA
role: The brain's main calming signal. It slows nerve activity down and is involved in anxiety, stress and sleep.
supportedBy: Sleep and exercise are linked to healthy GABA signalling. Alcohol acts on GABA, which is one reason it disturbs sleep and mood afterwards.

name: Melatonin
role: Released by the brain in response to darkness. It helps time your body clock and tells the body that it is night.
supportedBy: Bright light in the morning and dim light in the evening support a healthy melatonin rhythm. Screens and bright light late at night can delay it.

name: Adenosine
role: Builds up in the brain the longer you are awake and makes you feel sleepy. It clears while you sleep. Caffeine works by blocking it.
supportedBy: A full night of sleep clears adenosine. Caffeine late in the day hides sleepiness without removing it.

name: Vitamin D
role: Made in the skin from sunlight and also found in some foods. It is needed for bones, muscles, nerves and the immune system. Low vitamin D has been associated with low mood, although studies do not show that supplements treat depression.
supportedBy: Time outdoors in daylight, oily fish, eggs and fortified foods. In winter at northern latitudes the sun is too weak for the skin to make much.

name: Vitamin B12
role: Keeps blood and nerve cells healthy and helps make DNA. Low B12 is linked to tiredness, weakness and low mood.
supportedBy: Found in meat, fish, eggs and dairy, and in fortified foods. People who eat no animal products usually need fortified foods or a supplement.

name: Iron
role: Used to make haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in the blood. Low iron is linked to tiredness, weakness and trouble concentrating.
supportedBy: Found in meat, beans, lentils, spinach and fortified cereals. Regular meals make it easier to get enough.

name: Thyroid hormones
role: Set the pace of your metabolism: how fast the body uses energy. Too little is linked to tiredness, feeling cold and low mood; too much is linked to anxiety and a fast heartbeat.
supportedBy: Thyroid levels are checked with a blood test. Lasting tiredness or mood changes are worth mentioning to a GP.
